Then, multiplying both sides of Equation S2.9 by a factor of (-1)Nl\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{l}}$\end{document}, we get:(S2.10)(−1)NlΔ{1,...,Nl}(R)=−J12J23⋯JNl1+∑σ∈SNl∖{σc}(−1)Nl+κ(σ)Rσ(1)1Rσ(2)2⋯Rσ(Nl)Nl.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left (-1\right)^{N_{l}}\Delta _{\left \{1,...,N_{l}\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)=-J_{12}J_{23}\cdots J_{N_{l}1}+\sum _{\sigma \in \mathcal{S}_{N_{l}}\smallsetminus \left \{\sigma _{c}\right \}}\left (-1\right)^{N_{l}+\kappa \left (\sigma \right)}R_{\sigma \left (1\right)1}R_{\sigma \left (2\right)2}\cdots R_{\sigma \left (N_{l}\right)N_{l}}.$$\end{document}

As we mentioned before, the product J12J23⋯JNl1\begin{document}$J_{12}J_{23}\cdots J_{N_{l}1}$\end{document} is strictly positive by definition and hence, the first term in Equation S2.10 is strictly negative. Consequently, regardless of the sign of the second term, there always exists some choice of model parameters for which Equation S2.10 becomes negative, namely,(S2.11)J12J23⋯JNl1>∑σ∈SNl∖{σc}(−1)Nl+κ(σ)Rσ(1)1Rσ(2)2⋯Rσ(Nl)Nl.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle J_{12}J_{23}\cdots J_{N_{l}1}\gt \sum _{\sigma \in \mathcal{S}_{N_{l}}\smallsetminus \left \{\sigma _{c}\right \}}\left (-1\right)^{N_{l}+\kappa \left (\sigma \right)}R_{\sigma \left (1\right)1}R_{\sigma \left (2\right)2}\cdots R_{\sigma \left (N_{l}\right)N_{l}}.$$\end{document}

This means, according to Equation S2.5, that Δ1,...,Nl(R)\begin{document}$\Delta _{1,...,N_{l}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)$\end{document} is a destabilizing minor and thus, the proof of Lemma S2.1 is finished.

sec.title: Positive intracellular loops induce RD-instabilities of the second kind
sec.p: Let us consider a gene regulatory network with Nic≥1\begin{document}$N_{ic} \geq 1$\end{document} intracellular gene products and Nec=Ng-Nic\begin{document}$N_{ec}=N_{g}-N_{ic}$\end{document} extracellular signals, and let l+={j1,...,jNl}⊆{i1,...,iNic}\begin{document}$\text{l}^{\text{+}}=\left \{j_{1},...,j_{N_{l}}\right \}\subseteq \left \{i_{1},...,i_{N_{ic}}\right \}$\end{document} form a positive intracellular loop, with Nl≤Nic\begin{document}$N_{l}\leq N_{ic}$\end{document}. In accordance with Lemma S2.1, we know that the principal minor of R=R(0)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}=\boldsymbol{R}\left (0\right)$\end{document} associated with l+\begin{document}$\text{l}^{\text{+}}$\end{document} is a destabilizing minor, as it corresponds to a positive regulatory loop. The following results extend this property to the principal minor of R\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}$\end{document} associated with the whole set of intracellular gene products in the network (i.e. from {j1,...,jNl}\begin{document}$\left \{j_{1},...,j_{N_{l}}\right \}$\end{document} to {i1,...,iNic}\begin{document}$\left \{i_{1},...,i_{N_{ic}}\right \}$\end{document}):

Lemma S2.2. Let us consider a gene regulatory network with Ng>1\begin{document}$N_{g}\gt 1$\end{document} gene products and let {i1,...,iNic}\begin{document}$\left \{i_{1},...,i_{N_{ic}}\right \}$\end{document} denote its Nic<Ng\begin{document}$N_{ic} \lt N_{g}$\end{document} intracellular gene products. If such gene network exhibits at least one positive intracellular loop l+={j1,...,jNl}⊆{i1,...,iNic}\begin{document}$\text{l}^{\text{+}}=\left \{j_{1},...,j_{N_{l}}\right \}\subseteq \left \{i_{1},...,i_{N_{ic}}\right \}$\end{document}, with Nl≤Ng\begin{document}$N_{l}\leq N_{g}$\end{document}, then the principal minor of R=R(0)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}=\boldsymbol{R}\left (0\right)$\end{document} associated with {i1,...,iNic}\begin{document}$\left \{i_{1},...,i_{N_{ic}}\right \}$\end{document} is a destabilizing minor of R\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}$\end{document}.

Proof (of Lemma S2.2). Without loss of generality, we can assume that the Nic\begin{document}$N_{ic}$\end{document} intracellular gene products in the network are labeled {1,...,Nic}\begin{document}$\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}$\end{document}, with l+={1,...,Nl}\begin{document}$\text{l}^{+}=\left \{1,...,N_{l}\right \}$\end{document} (otherwise, we can reorder the labels in the gene network without changing its network topology). Moreover, for the sake of simplicity, we denote μ^i=miμi(gi*)mi−1\begin{document}$\hat {\mu }_{i}=m_{i}\mu _{i}\left (g_{i}^{\text{*}}\right)^{m_{i}-1}$\end{document} the degradation term corresponding to gene product i∈{1,...,Nic}\begin{document}$i\in \left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}$\end{document}.

From Lemma S2.1, we know that there exists some choice of model parameters such that (−1)NlΔl+(R)<0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{l}}\Delta _{\text{l}^{\text{+}}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right) \lt 0$\end{document}. Hence, if Nl=Nic\begin{document}$N_{l}=N_{ic}$\end{document}, Δ{1,...,Nic}(R)=Δl+(R)\begin{document}$\Delta _{\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)=\Delta _{\text{l}^{\text{+}}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)$\end{document} is trivially a destabilizing minor of R\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}$\end{document}. If Nl<Nic\begin{document}$N_{l} \lt N_{ic}$\end{document}, let i∈{Nl+1,...,Nic}\begin{document}$i\in \left \{N_{l}+1,...,N_{ic}\right \}$\end{document} be any intracellular gene product outside of l+\begin{document}$\text{l}^{\text{+}}$\end{document}. Then, using the minor decomposition formula (Strang, 2016), we can write Δl+∪{i}(R)=det(Rl+∪{i})\begin{document}$\Delta _{\text{l}^{\text{+}}{\cup }\left \{i\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)=\det\left (\boldsymbol{R}_{\text{l}^{\text{+}}{\cup }\left \{i\right \}}\right)$\end{document} in the form:(S2.12)Δl+∪{i}(R)=(Jii−μ^i)Δl+(R)+∑j∈l+(−1)Nl+1+jJijΔ(l+∖{j})∪{i}(R).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta _{\text{l}^{\text{+}}{\cup }\left \{i\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)=\left (J_{ii}-\hat {\mu }_{i}\right)\Delta _{\text{l}^{\text{+}}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\sum _{j\in \text{l}^{\text{+}}}\left (-1\right)^{N_{l}+1+j}J_{ij}\Delta _{\left (\text{l}^{\text{+}}\smallsetminus \left \{j\right \}\right){\cup }\left \{i\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right).$$\end{document}

If we now multiply both sides of Equation S2.12 by a factor of (-1)Nl+1\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{l}+1}$\end{document}, we get:(S2.13)(−1)Nl+1Δl+∪{i}(R)=−(Jii−μ^i)(−1)NlΔl+(R)+∑j∈l+(−1)jJijΔ(l+∖{j})∪{i}(R).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left (-1\right)^{N_{l}+1}\Delta _{\text{l}^{\text{+}}{\cup }\left \{i\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)=-\left (J_{ii}-\hat {\mu }_{i}\right)\left (-1\right)^{N_{l}}\Delta _{\text{l}^{\text{+}}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\sum _{j\in \text{l}^{\text{+}}}\left (-1\right)^{j}J_{ij}\Delta _{\left (\text{l}^{\text{+}}\smallsetminus \left \{j\right \}\right)\cup\left \{i\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right). $$\end{document}

However, we know that there exists some choice of model parameters for which (−1)NlΔl+(R)<0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{l}}\Delta _{\text{l}^{\text{+}}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right) \lt 0$\end{document} and then, complementing such choice with a set of model parameters for gene product i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} (i.e. Jii\begin{document}$J_{ii}$\end{document}, μ^i\begin{document}$\overset{\hat }{\mu }_{i}$\end{document}, and Jij\begin{document}$J_{ij}$\end{document} for all j∈l+\begin{document}$j\in \text{l}^{\text{+}}$\end{document}) such that(S2.14)(Jii−μ^i)<∑(−1)jJijΔ(l+∖{j})∪{i}(R)(−1)NlΔl+(R),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left (J_{ii}-\hat {\mu }_{i}\right) \lt \frac{\sum \left (-1\right)^{j}J_{ij}\Delta _{\left (\text{l}^{\text{+}}\smallsetminus \left \{j\right \}\right){\cup }\left \{i\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)}{\left (-1\right)^{N_{l}}\Delta _{\text{l}^{\text{+}}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)},$$\end{document}

we get (−1)Nl+1Δl+∪{i}(R)<0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{l}+1}\Delta _{\text{l}^{\text{+}}{\cup }\left \{i\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right) \lt 0$\end{document} (note that the sign of the terms in the top sum of the right-hand side of Equation S2.14 alternates depending on the parity of j\begin{document}$j$\end{document}). This means, according to Equation S2.25, that the principal minor Δl+∪{i}(R)\begin{document}$\Delta _{\text{l}^{\text{+}}{\cup }\left \{i\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)$\end{document} is a destabilizing minor of R\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}$\end{document}. Then, the same argument can be iteratively applied to the remaining gene products outside of l+∪{i}\begin{document}$\text{l}^{\text{+}}{\cup }\left \{i\right \}$\end{document} until we end up showing that Δ{1,...,Nic}(R)\begin{document}$\Delta _{\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)$\end{document} is indeed a destabilizing minor. This finishes the proof of Lemma S2.2.

So far, parameter choices involved in Lemmas S2.1 and S2.2 correspond exclusively to the reaction part of the reaction-diffusion equations (i.e. Jacobian entries Jij\begin{document}$J_{ij}$\end{document}, degradation coefficients μi\begin{document}$\mu _{i}$\end{document}, degradation orders mi\begin{document}$m_{i}$\end{document}, and steady-state concentrations gi*\begin{document}$g_{i}^{\text{*}}$\end{document}). Nevertheless, to understand the true role of positive loops in pattern transformation, we must examine the effect that destabilizing minors of R=R(0)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}=\boldsymbol{R}\left (0\right)$\end{document} have on the full reaction-diffusion matrix R(k2)=R−k2D\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}\left (\boldsymbol{k}^{2}\right)=\boldsymbol{R}-\boldsymbol{k}^{2}\boldsymbol{D}$\end{document}, for all wavenumbers k∈σ(∇2)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{k}{\in }\sigma \left ({\nabla }^{2}\right)$\end{document}. To do so, given that D\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{D}$\end{document} is by definition a positive semidefinite diagonal matrix, we can write the determinant of R(k2)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}\left (\boldsymbol{k}^{2}\right)$\end{document} in terms of the principal minors of R\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}$\end{document} as follows (Wang and Li, 2001):(S2.15)det(R(k2))=det(R)+∑j=1Ng−1((−1)j∑γ∈Ij(k2jΔγc(R)∏i∈γdi))+(−1)Ngk2Ng∏i=1Ngdi,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\left (\boldsymbol{k}^{2}\right)\right)=\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\sum _{j=1}^{N_{g}-1}\left (\left (-1\right)^{j}\sum _{\gamma \in \mathcal{I}_{j}}\left (\boldsymbol{k}^{2j}\Delta _{\gamma ^{c}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)\prod _{i\in \gamma }d_{i}\right)\right)+\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\boldsymbol{k}^{2N_{g}}\prod _{i=1}^{N_{g}}d_{i},$$\end{document}

where Ij={γ={i1,...,ij}/1≤i1≤...≤ij≤Ng}\begin{document}$\mathcal{I}_{j}=\left \{\gamma =\left \{i_{1},...,i_{j}\right \}/1\leq i_{1}\leq ...\leq i_{j}\leq N_{g}\right \}$\end{document} denotes the set of all j\begin{document}$j$\end{document}-element index sequences extracted from {1,...,Nq}\begin{document}$\left \{1,...,N_{q}\right \}$\end{document}, and γc={1,...,Ng}∖γ\begin{document}$\gamma ^{c}=\left \{1,...,N_{g}\right \}\smallsetminus \gamma $\end{document} is the complementary sequence of γ∈Ij\begin{document}$\gamma \in \mathcal{I}_{j}$\end{document}.

The following result shows that any gene network containing at least one positive intracellular loop admits at least one choice of model parameters (including diffusion coefficients in D\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{D}$\end{document}) for which it becomes an RD-unstable network of the second kind:

Proposition S2.3. Let us consider a gene regulatory network with Nic≥1\begin{document}$N_{ic}\geq 1$\end{document} intracellular gene products and Nec=Ng-Nic≥1\begin{document}$N_{ec}=N_{g}-N_{ic}\geq 1$\end{document} extracellular signals. If the network contains at least one positive intracellular loop l+={j1,...,jNl}\begin{document}$\text{l}^{\text{+}}=\left \{j_{1},...,j_{N_{l}}\right \}$\end{document}, with Nl≤Nic\begin{document}$N_{l}\leq N_{ic}$\end{document}, then, there exists a choice of model parameters for which the gene network becomes an RD-unstable network of the second kind.

Proof (of Proposition S2.3). Without loss of generality, we can assume that the Nic\begin{document}$N_{ic}$\end{document} intracellular gene products in the network are labeled {1,...,Nic}\begin{document}$\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}$\end{document}, with l+={1,...,Nl}\begin{document}$\text{l}^{\text{+}}=\left \{1,...,N_{l}\right \}$\end{document} (otherwise, we can reorder the labels in the gene network without changing its network topology). Moreover, for the sake of simplicity, we denote by μ^i=miμi(gi*)mi−1\begin{document}$\hat {\mu }_{i}=m_{i}\mu _{i}\left (g_{i}^{\text{*}}\right)^{m_{i}-1}$\end{document} the full degradation term corresponding to gene product i∈{1,...,Ng}\begin{document}$i\in \left \{1,...,N_{g}\right \}$\end{document}.

From Lemmas S2.1 and S2.2, we know that the principal minor of R=R(0)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}=\boldsymbol{R}\left (0\right)$\end{document} associated with the full set of intracellular gene products {1,...,Nic}\begin{document}$\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}$\end{document} is a destabilizing minor and consequently, that there exists a choice of model parameters for which(S2.16)(−1)NicΔ{1,...,Nic}(R)<0.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left (-1\right)^{N_{ic}}\Delta _{\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)\lt 0.$$\end{document}

First, we will focus on proving that there exists a choice of model parameters for which the gene network is RD-unstable, namely, a choice of model parameters for which there exists at least one unstable wavenumber k∈σ(∇2)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{k}\in \sigma \left ({\nabla }^{2}\right)$\end{document} for which its associated dispersion relation det(λI−R(k2))=0\begin{document}$\det \left (\lambda \boldsymbol{I}-\boldsymbol{R}\left (\boldsymbol{k}^{2}\right)\right)=0$\end{document} admits one solution with positive real part. In this sense, according to the Routh-Hurwitz conditions (Kurosh, 1984; Elsgolts, 2003), det(λI−R(k2))=0\begin{document}$\det \left (\lambda \boldsymbol{I}-\boldsymbol{R}\left (\boldsymbol{k}^{2}\right)\right)=0$\end{document} will admit a solution with positive real part if (−1)Ngdet(R(k2))<0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\left (\boldsymbol{k}^{2}\right)\right) \lt 0$\end{document}. Hence, it suffices to show that there exists some choice of model parameters for which this latter inequality holds to prove that the corresponding gene network is RD-unstable for such choice of model parameters.

Let k^≥0\begin{document}$\hat {k} \geq 0$\end{document} be a dummy continuous wavenumber variable. The determinant of R(k^)=R−k^D\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}\left (\hat {k}\right)=\boldsymbol{R}-\hat {k}\boldsymbol{D}$\end{document} can be written in terms of the minors of R\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}$\end{document} using Equation S2.15. However, since we have di=0\begin{document}$d_{i}=0$\end{document} for all i∈{1,...,Nic}\begin{document}$i\in \left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}$\end{document}, such formula reduces to:(S2.17)det(R(k^))=det(R)+(−1)Ng−Nick^Ng−NicΔ{1,...,Nic}(R)∏i=Nic+1Ngdi;\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\left (\hat {k}\right)\right)=\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}-N_{ic}}\hat {k}^{N_{g}-N_{ic}}\Delta _{\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)\prod _{i=N_{ic}+1}^{N_{g}}d_{i};$$\end{document}

and then, if we multiply both sides of Equation S2.17 by a factor of (-1)Ng\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}$\end{document}, we get:(S2.18)(−1)Ngdet(R(k^))=(−1)Ngdet(R)+(−1)Nick^Ng−NicΔ1,...,Nic(R)∏i=Nic+1Ngdi.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\left (\hat {k}\right)\right)=\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\left (-1\right)^{N_{ic}}\hat {k}^{N_{g}-N_{ic}}\Delta _{1,...,N_{ic}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)\prod _{i=N_{ic}+1}^{N_{g}}d_{i}.$$\end{document}

According to Equation S2.16, there exists some choice of model parameters for which (−1)NicΔ{1,...,Nic}(R)<0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{ic}}\Delta _{\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right) \lt 0$\end{document}. Thus, given that k^≥0\begin{document}$\hat {k} \geq 0$\end{document} and di>0\begin{document}$d_{i} \gt 0$\end{document} , for all i∈{Nic+1,...,Ng}\begin{document}$i\in \left \{N_{ic}+1,...,N_{g}\right \}$\end{document}, there exists some threshold wavenumber K^≥0\begin{document}$\hat {K}\geq 0$\end{document} such that (−1)Ngdet(R(k^))<0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\left (\hat {k}\right)\right) \lt 0$\end{document} for all k^>K^\begin{document}$\hat {k} \gt \hat {K}$\end{document}. Namely:(S2.19)K^=max{0,((−1)Nec+1det(R)Δ{1,...,Nic}(R)∏di)1Nec},\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat {K}=\max \left \{0,\left (\frac{\left (-1\right)^{N_{ec}+1}\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)}{\Delta _{\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)\prod d_{i}}\right)^{\frac{1}{N_{ec}}}\right \},$$\end{document}

sec.title: Positive extracellular loops induce RD-instabilities of the first kind
sec.p: Let us consider a gene regulatory network with Nec≥1\begin{document}$N_{ec}\geq 1$\end{document} extracellular signals and Nic=Ng-Nec≥0\begin{document}$N_{ic}=N_{g}-N_{ec}\geq 0$\end{document} intracellular gene products, and let L+={j1,...,jNl}\begin{document}$L^{\text{+}}=\left \{j_{1},...,j_{N_{l}}\right \}$\end{document} form the largest positive extracellular loop in the network (i.e. at least one gene product ji∈L+\begin{document}$j_{i}\text{\in }L^{\text{+}}$\end{document} is an extracellular signal). To isolate, and better understand, the role of positive extracellular loops in pattern transformation, we will assume for the remainder of this subsection that the gene networks under consideration do not contain any positive intracellular loop (the combination of positive extracellular and intracellular loops is considered in the following subsection). In particular, given this lack of positive intracellular loops in the network, we will have that the principal minor associated with the set of intracellular gene products {i1,...,iNic}\begin{document}$\left \{i_{1},...,i_{N_{ic}}\right \}$\end{document} is never a destabilizing minor. Hence, for any choice of model parameters, we have:(S2.20)(−1)NicΔ{i1,...,iNc}(R)>0.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left (-1\right)^{N_{ic}}\Delta _{\left \{i_{1},...,i_{N_{c}}\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)\gt 0.$$\end{document}

The following results show that, if a gene regulatory network whose positive loops are all extracellular becomes RD-unstable for some choice of model parameters, then it can only be an RD-unstable network of the first kind (i.e. its associated dispersion relation would yield only a finite number of unstable wavenumbers k∈σ(∇2)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{k}\in \sigma \left ({\nabla }^{2}\right)$\end{document}):

Proposition S2.4. Let us consider a gene regulatory network with Nec≥1\begin{document}$N_{ec}\geq 1$\end{document} extracellular signals and Nic=Ng-Nec≥0\begin{document}$N_{ic}=N_{g}-N_{ec}\geq 0$\end{document} intracellular gene products, and assume all positive loops in the network are extracellular, with L+={j1,...,jNl}\begin{document}$L^{\text{+}}=\left \{j_{1},...,j_{N_{l}}\right \}$\end{document} denoting the largest one; then, if there exists some choice of model parameters for which the network becomes RD-unstable, it can only be an RD-unstable network of the first kind.

Proof (of Proposition S2.4). Let U=L+∪{i1,...,iNic}\begin{document}$\text{U}=L^{\text{+}}{\cup }\left \{i_{1},...,i_{N_{ic}}\right \}$\end{document} be the union set of loop L+\begin{document}$L^{\text{+}}$\end{document} with the set of all intracellular gene products in the network {i1,...,iNic}\begin{document}$\left \{i_{1},...,i_{N_{ic}}\right \}$\end{document}, and let M=|U|\begin{document}$M=|{U}|$\end{document} be the number of elements in U\begin{document}$\text{U}$\end{document}. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the M\begin{document}$M$\end{document} gene products in U\begin{document}$\text{U}$\end{document} are labeled {1,...,M}\begin{document}$\left \{1,...,M\right \}$\end{document}, with intracellular gene products being {1,...,Nic}\begin{document}$\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}$\end{document} (otherwise, we can always reorder the labels in the gene network without changing its network topology). Moreover, for the sake of simplicity, we denote by μ^i=miμi(gi*)mi-1\begin{document}$\overset{\hat }{\mu }_{i}=m_{i}\mu _{i}\left (g_{i}^{\text{*}}\right)^{m_{i}-1}$\end{document} the full degradation term corresponding to gene product i∈{1,...,Ng}\begin{document}$i\in \left \{1,...,N_{g}\right \}$\end{document}.

From Lemma S2.1, we know that the principal minor of R=R(0)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}=\boldsymbol{R}\left (0\right)$\end{document} associated with L+\begin{document}$L^{\text{+}}$\end{document} is a destabilizing minor (i.e. there exists some choice of model parameters for which (−1)NlΔL+(R)<0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{l}}\Delta _{L^{\text{+}}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right) \lt 0$\end{document}). Moreover, proceeding as in Lemma S2.2, we can extend such property to the principal minor associated with U\begin{document}$\mathit{U} $\end{document}. Hence, we can find a choice of model parameters for which:(S2.21)(−1)MΔU(R)<0.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left (-1\right)^{M}\Delta _{\text{U}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)\lt 0.$$\end{document}

First, we will focus on showing that the positive extracellular loop L+\begin{document}$L^{\text{+}}$\end{document} enables the existence of some choice of model parameters for which the network is RD-unstable (i.e. for which its associated dispersion relation yields at least one unstable wavenumber k∈σ(∇2)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{k}\in \sigma \left ({\nabla }^{2}\right)$\end{document}). As in the proof of Proposition S2.3, we will do it using the Ruth-Hurwitz conditions (Kurosh, 1984; Elsgolts, 2003) to ensure that det(λI−R(k2))=0\begin{document}$\det \left (\lambda \boldsymbol{I}-\boldsymbol{R}\left (\boldsymbol{k}^{2}\right)\right)=0$\end{document} has at least one solution with positive real part by ensuring that (−1)Ngdet(R(k2))<0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\left (\boldsymbol{k}^{2}\right)\right) \lt 0$\end{document}.

Let k^≥0\begin{document}$\hat {k} \geq 0$\end{document} be a dummy continuous wavenumber variable, and let us take di=δ>0\begin{document}$d_{i}=\delta \gt 0$\end{document} for all extracellular signal i∈{Nic+1,...,Ng}\begin{document}$i\in \left \{N_{ic}+1,...,N_{g}\right \}$\end{document}. The determinant of R(k^)=R−k^D\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}\left (\hat {k}\right)=\boldsymbol{R}-\hat {k}\boldsymbol{D}$\end{document} can be written in terms of the minors of R\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{R}$\end{document} using Equation S2.15. Indeed, if δ\begin{document}$\delta $\end{document} is small enough, we have:(S2.22)det(R(k^))=det(R)+(−1)Ng−M(k^δ)Ng−MΔU(R)+O(δ),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\left (\hat {k}\right)\right)=\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}-M}\left (\hat {k}\delta \right)^{N_{g}-M}\Delta _{\text{U}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\mathcal{O}\left (\delta \right),$$\end{document}

where O(δ)\begin{document}$\mathcal{O}\left (\delta \right)$\end{document} represents Landau’s big-O notation. Then, if we multiply both sides of Equation S2.22 by a factor of (-1)Ng\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}$\end{document}, we get:(S2.23)(−1)Ngdet(R(k^))=(−1)Ngdet(R)+(−1)M(k^δ)Ng−MΔU(R)+O(δ).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\det\left (\boldsymbol{R}\left (\hat {k}\right)\right)=\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\det\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\left (-1\right)^{M}\left (\hat k\delta \right)^{N_{g}-M}\Delta _{\text{U}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\mathcal{O}\left (\delta \right).$$\end{document}

According to Equation S2.21, there exists some choice of model parameters for which (−1)MΔU(R)<0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{M}\Delta _{\text{U}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right) \lt 0$\end{document}. Hence, if δ\begin{document}$\delta $\end{document} is small enough, it is possible to find some lower bound K^L≥0\begin{document}$\overset{\hat }{K}_{L}\geq 0$\end{document} such that (−1)Ngdet(R(k2))<0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\left (\boldsymbol{k}^{2}\right)\right) \lt 0$\end{document} for some wavenumber k∈σ(∇2)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{k}{\in }\sigma \left ({\nabla }^{2}\right)$\end{document} with k2≥K^L\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{k}^{2} \geq \hat {K}_{L}$\end{document}. Namely:(S2.24)K^L≃max{0,1δ((−1)Ng−M−1det(R)ΔU(R))1Ng−M).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat {K}_{L}{\simeq max}\left \{0,\frac{1}{\delta }\left (\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}-M-1}\frac{\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)}{\Delta _{U}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)}\right)^{\frac{1}{N_{g}-M}}\right).$$\end{document}

Nonetheless, in contrast to Proposition S2.3, the squared wavenumber k2\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{k}^{2}$\end{document} cannot be taken arbitrarily bigger than K^L\begin{document}$\overset{\hat }{K}_{L}$\end{document} as higher order terms within O(δ)\begin{document}$\mathcal{O}\left (\delta \right)$\end{document} may become relevant and alter the sign of (−1)Ngdet(R(k2))\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\left (\boldsymbol{k}^{2}\right)\right)$\end{document}. To illustrate this, let us extract the term of order k^Ng−Nic\begin{document}$\hat {k}^{N_{g}-N_{ic}}$\end{document} from O(δ)\begin{document}$\mathcal{O}\left (\delta \right)$\end{document} in Equation S2.23 and get:(S2.25)(−1)Ngdet(R(k^))=(−1)Ngdet(R)+(−1)M(k^δ)Ng−MΔU(R)+(−1)Nic(k^δ)Ng−NicΔ{1,...,Nic}(R)+O(δ),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\left (\hat {k}\right)\right)=\left (-1\right)^{N_{g}}\det \left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\left (-1\right)^{M}\left (\hat {k}\delta \right)^{N_{g}-M}\Delta _{\text{U}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\left (-1\right)^{N_{ic}}\left (\hat {k}\delta \right)^{N_{g}-N_{ic}}\Delta _{\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)+\mathcal{O}\left (\delta \right),$$\end{document}

where, in virtue of Equation S2.20, (−1)NicΔ{1,...,Nic}(R)>0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{ic}}\Delta _{\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right) \gt 0$\end{document} for any choice of model parameters. Thus, given that M>Nic\begin{document}$M \gt N_{ic}$\end{document}, we have that δ\begin{document}$\delta $\end{document} can always be taken small enough so that the third term in Equation S2.25 is negligible with respect to the second one. However, for any fixed value of δ\begin{document}$\delta $\end{document}, this third term (with order k^Ng−Nic\begin{document}$\hat{k}^{N_{g}-N_{ic}}$\end{document} and positive sign) will dominate over the second term (with order k^Ng−Nic\begin{document}$\hat{k}^{N_{g}-N_{ic}}$\end{document} and negative sign) if we let k^→∞\begin{document}$\hat {k}\rightarrow \infty $\end{document}. In particular, this means that one can always find some upper limit K^R≥0\begin{document}$\overset{\hat }{K}_{R}\geq 0$\end{document} such that:(S2.26)(−1)Nic(k^δ)Ng−NicΔ{1,...,Nic}(R)>|(−1)M(k^δ)Ng−MΔU(R)|,for allk^≥K^R.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left (-1\right)^{N_{ic}}\left (\hat {k}\delta \right)^{N_{g}-N_{ic}}\Delta _{\left \{1,...,N_{ic}\right \}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)\,\gt \, \left|\left (-1\right)^{M}\left (\hat {k}\delta \right)^{N_{g}-M}\Delta _{\text{U}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right)\right|,\text{for all}\,\hat{k}\geq \hat {K}_{R}.$$\end{document}

Finally, two observations are worth being made. First, note that tuning model parameters to get an RD-unstable network of the first kind generally requires a much finer degree of adjustment than that needed to get an RD-unstable network of the second kind. In the former case, one must find some wavenumber k∈σ(∇2)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{k}{\in }\sigma \left ({\nabla }^{2}\right)$\end{document} such that k2∈[K^L,K^R]\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{k}^{2}{\in } [\hat{K}_{L},\hat{K}_{R}]$\end{document}, where K^L\begin{document}$\hat {K}_{L}$\end{document} and K^R\begin{document}$\hat {K}_{R}$\end{document} are given in the proof of Proposition S2.4. Conversely, in the latter case it suffices to select a sufficiently large k∈σ(∇2)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{k}{\in }\sigma \left ({\nabla }^{2}\right)$\end{document} such that k2≥K^\begin{document}$k^{2} \geq \hat {K}$\end{document}, with K^\begin{document}$\hat {K}$\end{document} given by Equation S2.19.

On the other hand, it is worth recalling that although the parameter selection employed for the proof of Proposition S2.4 may appear rather artificial, instances of RD-unstable networks of the first kind arising from less convoluted parameter choices have been reported both in this article (e.g. Figures 8 and 9 in the main text) and in the literature (e.g. Gierer and Meinhardt, 1972; Murray, 2002; Levine and Rappel, 2005).

sec.title: Combination of positive extracellular and intracellular loops
sec.p: Let us consider a gene regulatory network with Nic≥1\begin{document}$N_{ic}\geq 1$\end{document} intracellular gene products and Nec=Ng-Nic≥1\begin{document}$N_{ec}=N_{g}-N_{ic}\geq 1$\end{document} extracellular signals, and let l+={i1,...,iNl}\begin{document}$\text{l}^{\text{+}}=\left \{i_{1},...,i_{N_{l}}\right \}$\end{document} and L+={j1,...,jNl`}\begin{document}$L^{\text{+}}=\left \{j_{1},...,j_{N_{l}'}\right \}$\end{document} represent a positive intracellular loop and a positive extracellular loop, respectively. Given that the network contains at least one positive intracellular loop, Proposition S2.3 guarantees the existence of some choice of model parameters for which the network becomes RD-unstable of the second kind. In such parameter set, the intracellular loop l+\begin{document}$\text{l}^{\text{+}}$\end{document} is effectively overweighted relative to the extracellular loop L+\begin{document}$L^{\text{+}}$\end{document}, thereby exerting a stronger influence on the corresponding pattern transformation.

However, model parameters may alternatively be tuned so as to satisfy (−1)NicΔi1,...,iNic(R)>0\begin{document}$\left (-1\right)^{N_{ic}}\Delta _{i_{1},...,i_{N_{ic}}}\left (\boldsymbol{R}\right) \gt 0$\end{document}. In this case, Proposition S2.4 ensures that this parameter set can be completed to a choice of model parameters for which the network becomes RD-unstable of the first kind. Under these conditions, the extracellular loop L+\begin{document}$L^{\text{+}}$\end{document} becomes overweighted relative to the intracellular loop l+\begin{document}$\text{l}^{\text{+}}$\end{document}, and consequently dominates the reaction-diffusion dynamics, leading to a bigger influence on the corresponding pattern transformation.

Thus, gene regulatory networks that combine positive extracellular and intracellular loops can exhibit RD-instabilities of either type, depending on the specific choice of model parameters. As a result, such networks have access to the full spectrum of pattern transformations associated with both classes of RD-unstable networks.

sec.title: S3: Gradients of extracellular signals from spikes
sec.p: In this section, we analyze the pattern transformations produced by a simple 2-node gene network consisting of a self-activating intracellular gene product, denoted 1, that activates an extracellular signal, denoted A\begin{document}$A$\end{document}, when acting on a 1D spike initial pattern. As described in the main text, extracellular signals in this situation are secreted from the spike and form exponential gradients whose slopes depend on model parameters such as their diffusion and degradation coefficients. This subsection therefore provides a detailed derivation of Equation 24 in the main text.

We begin by solving for a stationary concentration of intracellular gene product 1. The concentration dynamics of this intracellular gene product for each x\begin{document}$x$\end{document} is given by the following initial value problem (recall Equation 1 in the main text):(S3.1){∂tg1(t,x)=f1(g1(t,x))−μ1g1(t,x),g1(0,x)=A1rect(|x−x0|L),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left\{\begin{array}{ll}\partial _{t}g_{1}\left (t,x\right)=f_{1}\left (g_{1}\left (t,x\right)\right)-\mu _{1}g_{1}\left (t,x\right),\\ g_{1}\left (0,x\right)=A_{1}\text{rect}\left (\frac{|x-x_{0}|}{L}\right),\end{array}\right.$$\end{document}

where A1>0\begin{document}$A_{1} \gt 0$\end{document} is the small amplitude of the spike, L>0\begin{document}$L \gt 0$\end{document} is its width, and rect(y)\begin{document}$\text{rect}\left (y\right)$\end{document} denotes the rectangular functions, i.e., rect(y)=1\begin{document}$\text{rect}\left (y\right)=1$\end{document}, if −1≤y≤1\begin{document}$-1 \leq y \leq 1$\end{document}, and rect(y)=0\begin{document}$\text{rect}\left (y\right)=0$\end{document}, otherwise (Abramowitz and Stegun, 1964). Without loss of generality, we can assume that the spike is centered at the origin x0=0\begin{document}$x_{0}=0$\end{document} (otherwise, we can simply consider a spatial translation of the problem).

For any position outside the spike (i.e. x∉[-L,L]\begin{document}$x\notin \left [-L,L\right ]$\end{document}), we have g1(t,x)=0\begin{document}$g_{1}\left (t,x\right)=0$\end{document} for all t>0\begin{document}$t \gt 0$\end{document}, since no production of gene product 1 can ever occur without any non-zero initial concentration and gene product 1 is regulated by no extracellular signal. On the contrary, for any position inside the spike x∈[-L,L]\begin{document}$x\in \left [-L,L\right ]$\end{document}, we have, up to a linear level:(S3.2)g1(t,x)=A1e(J11-μ1)t,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle g_{1}\left (t,x\right)=A_{1}e^{\left (J_{11}-\mu _{1}\right)t},$$\end{document}

where J11=∂g1f1(0)\begin{document}$J_{11}=\partial _{g_{1}}f_{1}\left (0\right)$\end{document}. Then, if μ1<J11\begin{document}$\mu _{1} \lt J_{11}$\end{document}, the concentration of gene product 1 inside the spike will grow away from 0 until it eventually saturates at some G1>0\begin{document}$G_{1} \gt 0$\end{document} due to the effect of the non-linear terms of f1(g1)\begin{document}$f_{1}\left (g_{1}\right)$\end{document} (recall requirements R2 and R4 in the main text). As a result, the resulting pattern of gene product 1 is a spike centered at the same position and a different height:(S3.3)g¯1(x)=G1rect(x/L).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar{g}_{1}\left (x\right)=G_{1}\text{rect}\left (x\text{/}L\right).$$\end{document}

Now, we turn to the analysis of pattern transformations in extracellular signal A. If we assume that gene product 1 reaches its stationary concentration fast enough, the concentration dynamics of signal A is given by (recall Equation 1 in the main text):(S3.4){∂tgA(t,x)−dA∂xx2gA(t,x)=−μAgA(t,x)+G^1rect(xL),lim|x|→∞gA(t,x)=0, and gA(0,x)=0,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left \{\begin{array}{l}\partial _{t}g_{A}\left (t,x\right)-d_{A}\partial _{xx}^{2}g_{A}\left (t,x\right)=-\mu _{A}g_{A}\left (t,x\right)+\hat {G}_{1}\text{rect}\left (\frac{x}{L}\right),\\\underset{|x|\rightarrow \infty }{\mathit{lim}} g_{A}\left (t,x\right)=0,\text{ and }g_{A}\left (0,x\right)=0,\end{array}\right.$$\end{document}

where G^1=fA(G1)\begin{document}$\hat {G}_{1}=f_{A}\left (G_{1}\right)$\end{document}. Solutions to a partial differential equation like Equation S3.4 can be written in the form gA(t,x)=gAHom(t,x)+g¯A(x)\begin{document}$g_{A}\left (t,x\right)=g_{A}^{Hom}\left (t,x\right)+\bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right)$\end{document} (Sneddon, 1957), where gAHom(t,x)\begin{document}$g_{A}^{Hom}\left (t,x\right)$\end{document} is a solution to the transient homogeneous equation:(S3.5){∂tgAHom(t,x)−dA∂xx2gAHom(t,x)+μAgAHom(t,x)=0;lim|x|→∞gAHom(t,x)=0, and gAHom(0,x)=−g¯A(x);\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left \{\begin{array}{l}\partial _{t}g_{A}^{Hom}\left (t,x\right)-d_{A}\partial _{xx}^{2}g_{A}^{Hom}\left (t,x\right)+\mu _{A}g_{A}^{Hom}\left (t,x\right)=0;\\\underset{|x|\rightarrow \infty }{\mathit{lim}} g_{A}^{Hom}\left (t,x\right)=0,\text{ and }g_{A}^{Hom}\left (0,x\right)=-\,\bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right);\end{array}\right.$$\end{document}

and g¯A(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right)$\end{document} is a solution to the stationary equation:(S3.6){∂xx2gA¯(x)=G^1dArect(xL)−μAdAg¯A(x),lim|x|→∞g¯A(t,x)=0.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left \{\begin{array}{l}\partial _{xx}^{2}\bar{g_{A}}\left (x\right)=\frac{\hat {G}_{1}}{d_{A}}\text{rect}\left (\frac{x}{L}\right)-\frac{\mu _{A}}{d_{A}}\bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right),\\\underset{|x|\rightarrow \infty }{\mathit{lim}} \bar{g}_{A}\left (t,x\right)=0.\end{array}\right.$$\end{document}

However, for the purposes of this article, we are just interested in the formation of stationary solutions of Equation S3.4 and thus, we can assume that limgAHom(t,x)=0\begin{document}${\mathit{lim}} g_{A}^{Hom}\left (t,x\right)=0$\end{document} and ignore Equation S3.5. Regarding the stationary equation, note that Equation S3.6 is invariant to sign reflection and so, g¯A(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right)$\end{document} must be an even function (i.e. g¯A(x)=g¯A(−x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right)=\bar{g}_{A}\left (-x\right)$\end{document}). Consequently, we must have ∂xg¯A(0)=0\begin{document}$\partial _{x}\bar{g}_{A}\left (0\right)=0$\end{document}, and we can restrict our search for a closed form of g¯A(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right)$\end{document} to only the right half-line (i.e. x≥0\begin{document}$x\geq 0$\end{document}) by adding the extra zero flux boundary condition ∂xg¯A(0)=0\begin{document}$\partial _{x}\bar{g}_{A}\left (0\right)=0$\end{document} to Equation S3.6.

In this sense, for positions within the spike (i.e. 0≤x≤L\begin{document}$0\leq x\leq L$\end{document}), rect(x/L)=1\begin{document}$\text{rect}\left (x/L\right)=1$\end{document} and Equation S3.6 reads:(S3.7){∂x2g¯A(x)=G^1dA−μAdAg¯A(x),∂xg¯A(0)=0, and g¯A(L)=B,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left \{\begin{array}{l}\partial _{x}^{2}\bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right)=\frac{\hat{G}_{1}}{d_{A}}-\frac{\mu _{A}}{d_{A}}\,\bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right),\\\partial _{x}\bar{g}_{A}\left (0\right)=0,\text{ and }\bar{g}_{A}\left (L\right)=B,\end{array}\right.$$\end{document}

where B∈R\begin{document}$B\in R$\end{document} is a splicing constant that we must later find. Solutions to Equation S3.7 are given by downward-facing hyperbolic cosines of the form:(S3.8)g¯A(x)=(B−G^1μA)\ cosh(ωAx)cosh(ωAL)\ +\ G^1μA,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right)=\left (B-\frac{\hat {G}_{1}}{\mu _{A}}\right)\text{\ }\frac{cosh\left (\omega _{A}x\right)}{cosh\left (\omega _{A}L\right)}\text{\ }+\text{\ }\frac{\hat {G}_{1}}{\mu _{A}},$$\end{document}

where ωA=μA/dA\begin{document}$\omega _{A}=\sqrt{\mu _{A}\text{/}d_{A}}$\end{document}. On the other hand, for positions outside the spike (i.e. x>L\begin{document}$x \gt L$\end{document}), rect(x/L)=0\begin{document}$\text{rect}\left (x/L\right)=0$\end{document} and then Equation S3.6 reduces to:(S3.9){∂xx2g¯A(x)=−μAdAg¯A(x),g¯A(L)=B, and limx→∞g¯A(x)=0,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left\{\begin{array}{l}\partial _{xx}^{2}\bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right)=-\frac{\mu _{A}}{d_{A}}\,\bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right),\\\bar{g}_{A}\left (L\right)=B,\text{ and }\underset{x\rightarrow \infty }{\mathit{lim}} \bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right)=0,\end{array}\right.$$\end{document}

where B\begin{document}$B$\end{document} is the same splicing constant as in Equation S3.7. Then, solutions to Equation S3.9 are given by a negative exponential of the form:(S3.10)g¯A(x)=Be−ωA(x−L).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right)=Be^{-\omega _{A} \left (x-L\right)}.$$\end{document}

By definition, solutions (Equation S3.8) and (Equation S3.10) match continuously at x=L\begin{document}$x=L$\end{document}. However, we can push this matching to be not only continuous but also continuously differentiable (i.e. class C1\begin{document}$\text{C}^{1}$\end{document}) by equating the first derivative of both functions at x=L\begin{document}$x=L$\end{document}, and solving for a closed form of the splicing constant B\begin{document}$B$\end{document}. Hence, after some algebra, we get:(S3.11)B=KA2(1−e−2ωAL),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle B=\frac{K_{A}}{2} \left (1-e^{-2\omega _{A}L}\right),$$\end{document}

where KA=G^1/μA\begin{document}$K_{A}=\hat {G}_{1}\text{/}\mu _{A}$\end{document}. Finally, if we substitute Equation S3.11 back into Equations S3.8 and Equations S3.10, we get that the stationary concentration of extracellular signal A\begin{document}$A$\end{document} is given by:(S3.12)g¯A(x)={KA(1−e−ωALcosh(ωAx)),if x∈[−L,L];KA2(1−e−2ωAL)e−ωA(|x|−L),otherwise.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar{g}_{A}\left (x\right)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll}K_{A}\left (1-e^{-\omega _{A}L}cosh\left (\omega _{A}x\right)\right), & \text{if } x\in \left [-L,L\right ];\\\frac{K_{A}}{2}\left (1-e^{-2\omega _{A}L}\right)e^{-\omega _{A}\left (|x|-L\right)}, & \text{otherwise.}\end{array}\right.$$\end{document}

As we can see, the stationary concentration of extracellular signal A\begin{document}$A$\end{document} exhibits a unique, symmetric concentration peak centered at the initial spike (x0=0\begin{document}$x_{0}=0$\end{document} in our case), and two gradients of exponential decay on both sides of the spike. The steepness of such gradients is controlled by parameter ωA\begin{document}$\omega _{A}$\end{document} (i.e. the square root of the ratio between the degradation rate and the diffusion rate) in the sense that the smaller ωA\begin{document}$\omega _{A}$\end{document} is, the steeper the corresponding gradient. Similarly, constant C\begin{document}$C$\end{document} in Equation 24 of the main text corresponds to:(S3.13)C=KA2(1−e−2ωAL)=G^12μA(1−e−2μAdAL).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle C=\frac{K_{A}}{2}\left (1-e^{-2\omega _{A}L}\right)=\frac{\hat {G}_{1}}{2\mu _{A}}\left (1-e^{-2\sqrt{\frac{\mu _{A}}{d_{A}}} L}\right).$$\end{document}

Here, we focus exclusively on the 1D pattern transformations in signal A. However, Equation S3.4 corresponds to the classical Helmholtz equation, whose solutions in higher dimensions are well known and extensively documented in the literature (Sommerfeld, 1949; Stakgold and Holst, 2011). Hence, we know that in 2D the signal concentration gradient outside the spike in Equation S3.12 decays as ∼e−||x||2/||x||2\begin{document}${\sim }e^{-||\boldsymbol{x}||_{2}}\text{/}\sqrt{||\boldsymbol{x}||_{2}}$\end{document}, where ||x||2\begin{document}$||\boldsymbol{x}||_{2}$\end{document} denotes the Euclidean norm, whereas in 3D, the corresponding gradient decays as ∼e−||x||2/||x||2\begin{document}${\sim }e^{-||\boldsymbol{x}||_{2}}\text{/}||\boldsymbol{x}||_{2}$\end{document}.

sec.title: S4: Pattern transformations in diamond gene networks for spike initial patterns
sec.p: In this section, we discuss some details of the 1D pattern transformations that a diamond gene network is able to produce when acting on spike initial patterns. We focus on the diamond network because its topology is simple enough to allow for a precise analysis of the pattern formation process, while remaining versatile enough to serve as a representative example of many of the features exhibited by more general hierarchical networks.

By definition, a diamond network consists of five distinct gene products (see Figure 12 in the main text). Specifically, it comprises an upstream intracellular gene product (denoted 1) that self-activates and activates two different extracellular signals (denoted 2 and 3). These signals regulate a common downstream intracellular gene product (denoted 4) in such a way that 2 activates 4 whereas 3 inhibits it. Finally, a fifth intracellular gene product (denoted 5) is directly activated by gene product 4. Moreover, we will assume that all gene products suffer from linear degradation (i.e. mi=1\begin{document}$m_{i}=1$\end{document} for all i∈{1,2,3,4,5}\begin{document}$i\in \left \{1,2,3,4,5\right \}$\end{document}).

As we saw in the previous section, extracellular signals 2 and 3 develop a resulting pattern consisting of a unique concentration peak centered at the spike and with exponential decay. Although this does not constitute a non-trivial pattern transformation (it fails to meet requirements Equations S1.5 and Equations S1.6), the fact that the resulting pattern is heterogeneous, and spreads along the domain due to signal diffusion, allows the emergence of non-trivial pattern transformations in downstream gene products 4 and 5.

The concentration dynamics of intracellular gene product 4 for each x\begin{document}$x$\end{document} is given by the following initial value problem (recall Equation 1 in the main text):(S4.1){∂tg4(t,x)=f4(g2(t,x),g3(t,x))−μ4g4(t,x),g4(0,x)=0.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left \{\begin{array}{l}\partial _{t}g_{4}\left (t,x\right)=f_{4}\left (g_{2}\left (t,x\right),g_{3}\left (t,x\right)\right)-\mu _{4}g_{4}\left (t,x\right),\\g_{4}\left (0,x\right)=0.\end{array}\right.$$\end{document}

Taking the time derivative in Equation S4.1 equal to zero, we can easily see that the stationary concentration of gene product 4 is given by:(S4.2)g¯4(x)=1μ4\ f4(g¯2(x),g¯3(x)),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)=\frac{1}{\mu _{4}}\text{\ }f_{4}\left (\bar{g}_{2}\left (x\right),\bar{g}_{3}\left (x\right)\right),$$\end{document}

where we have assumed that both extracellular signals reach their stationary concentrations g¯2(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{2}\left (x\right)$\end{document} and g¯3(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{3}\left (x\right)$\end{document} in Equation S3.12 fast enough. From requirement R5 in the main text, we know that f4(g2,g3)\begin{document}$f_{4}\left (g_{2},g_{3}\right)$\end{document} is monotonically increasing with respect to g2\begin{document}$g_{2}$\end{document} and monotonically decreasing with respect to g3\begin{document}$g_{3}$\end{document}. Then, if we focus on positions to the right of the spike (i.e. x>L\begin{document}$x \gt L$\end{document}) where both g¯2(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{2}\left (x\right)$\end{document} and g¯3(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{3}\left (x\right)$\end{document} display an exponential gradient, model parameters can be tuned so that the inhibition of 4 by 3 is larger than its activation by 2 close to the spike, and smaller further away. As a result, a concentration peak in the stationary concentration of 4 will emerge at some position x^>L\begin{document}$\hat {x} \gt L$\end{document} (and, by symmetry of Equation S3.12, also at x^<−L\begin{document}$\hat {x} \lt -L$\end{document}).

To illustrate this, let us consider the simple case in which f4(gA,gB)=W24g2-W34g3\begin{document}$f_{4}\left (g_{A},g_{B}\right)=W_{24}g_{2}-W_{34}g_{3}$\end{document} is a linear function, where W24,W34>0\begin{document}$W_{24},W_{34} \gt 0$\end{document} represent the weights of the regulations that 2 and 3 exert on 4, respectively. In this scenario, Equation S4.2 reduces to:(S4.3)g¯4(x)=12μ4(W24K2(1-e-2ω2L) e-ω2(x-L)-W34K3(1-e-2ω3L) e-ω3(x-L)),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)=\frac{1}{2\mu _{4}}\left (W_{24}K_{2}\left (1-e^{-2\omega _{2}L}\right)\text{\ }e^{-\omega _{2}\left (x-L\right)}-W_{34}K_{3}\left (1-e^{-2\omega _{3}L}\right)\text{\ }e^{-\omega _{3}\left (x-L\right)}\right),$$\end{document}

for all positions to the right of the spike (i.e. x>L\begin{document}$x \gt L$\end{document}). Hence, if we take the first spatial derivative of Equation S4.3, we get:(S4.4)∂xg¯4(x)=-12μ4(W24K2ω2(1-e-2ω2L) e-ω2(x-L)-W34K3ω3(1-e-2ω3L) e-ω3(x-L));\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \partial _{x}\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)=\frac{-1}{2\mu _{4}}\left (W_{24}K_{2}\omega _{2}\left (1-e^{-2\omega _{2}L}\right)\text{\ }e^{-\omega _{2}\left (x-L\right)}-W_{34}K_{3}\omega _{3}\left (1-e^{-2\omega _{3}L}\right)\text{\ }e^{-\omega _{3}\left (x-L\right)}\right);$$\end{document}

and thus, taking ∂xg¯4(x)=0\begin{document}$\partial_{x}\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)=0$\end{document} in Equation S4.4, we can derive a closed form for a unique critical point of g¯4(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_4\left (x\right)$\end{document} on the right-hand side of the initial spike given by:(S4.5)x^=L+1ω3−ω2log(W34K3ω3W24K2ω21−e−2ω3L1−e−2ω2L).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat {x}=L+\frac{1}{\omega _{3}-\omega _{2}}log\left (\frac{W_{34}K_{3}\omega _{3}}{W_{24}K_{2}\omega _{2}}\frac{1-e^{-2\omega _{3}L}}{1-e^{-2\omega _{2}L}}\right).$$\end{document}

However, this critical point is only formal, as its existence relies on a choice of model parameters for which x^>L\begin{document}$\hat {x} \gt L$\end{document}. In this sense, after some computations on Equation S4.5, we can see that this is the case for any parameter set that satisfies:(S4.6)ω3>ω2,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \omega _{3} \gt \omega _{2},$$\end{document}

so that the fraction in the second term of Equation S4.5 is positive, and:(S4.7)W34K3ω3W24K2ω2>1−e−2ω2L1−e−2ω3L,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{W_{34}K_{3}\omega _{3}}{W_{24}K_{2}\omega _{2}} \gt \frac{1-e^{-2\omega _{2}L}}{1-e^{-2\omega _{3}L}},$$\end{document}

so that the logarithm in the second term of Equation S4.5 is also positive. Then, if Equation S4.6 and Equation S4.7 hold, we have ∂xg¯4(x)>0\begin{document}$\partial _{x}\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right) \gt 0$\end{document} for all positions between x=L\begin{document}$x=L$\end{document} and x=x^>L\begin{document}$x=\hat {x} \gt L$\end{document}, while ∂xg¯4(x)<0\begin{document}$\partial _{x}\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right) \lt 0$\end{document} for all positions larger than x=x^\begin{document}$x=\hat {x}$\end{document}. Consequently, x^\begin{document}$\hat {x}$\end{document} is a concentration peak of g¯4(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)$\end{document} and, thus, we can conclude that gene product undergoes a non-trivial pattern transformation given by the emergence of such concentration peak to the right of the initial spike. In fact, given the parity of Equation S3.12, we know that a symmetric concentration peak of g¯4(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)$\end{document} also emerges at x=−x^\begin{document}$x=-\hat {x}$\end{document}, to the left of the spike.

Finally, the concentration dynamics of intracellular gene product 5 for each position x\begin{document}$x$\end{document} is given by the initial value problem (recall Equation 1 in the main text):(S4.8){∂tg5(t,x)=f5(g4(t,x))−μ5g5(t,x),g5(0,x)=0.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \left \{\begin{array}{l}\partial _{t}g_{5}\left (t,x\right)=f_{5}\left (g_{4}\left (t,x\right)\right)-\mu _{5}g_{5}\left (t,x\right),\\g_{5}\left (0,x\right)=0.\end{array}\right.$$\end{document}

Then, if we set the time derivative in Equation S4.8 equal to zero, we can easily see that the stationary concentration of gene product 5 is given by:(S4.9)g¯5(x)=1μ5f5(g¯4(x)),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar{g}_{5} (x)=\frac{1}{\mu _{5}}f_{5}\left (\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)\right),$$\end{document}

where we have assumed that gene product 4 reaches its stationary concentration g¯4(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)$\end{document} fast enough. We know from R5 in the main text, that f5(g4)\begin{document}$f_{5}\left (g_{4}\right)$\end{document} must preserve the monotony of g¯4(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)$\end{document} (i.e. it must increase where g¯4(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)$\end{document} increases, and decrease where g¯4(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)$\end{document} decreases). As a result, the resulting pattern of 5 replicates the resulting pattern of 4 in the sense that concentration peaks and valleys in g¯5(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{5}\left (x\right)$\end{document} are located at the same positions as those of g¯4(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{4}\left (x\right)$\end{document}. Nonetheless, by tuning the functional form of f5(g4)\begin{document}$f_{5}\left (g_{4}\right)$\end{document}, as well as the value of model parameters like μ5\begin{document}$\mu _{5}$\end{document}, we can make the concentration peaks and valleys of 5 higher, deeper, or steeper than those of 4.

All in all, we have proven that a simple diamond H network is enough to transform a spike initial pattern into a resulting pattern with two symmetric peaks of concentrations on both sides of the initial pattern. Moreover, as suggested by Equation S4.5 and Equation S4.9, model parameters and function f\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{f}$\end{document} can be tuned to make such concentration peaks appear at any position out of the spike, and have any desired height and steepness.

sec.title: S5: Peak addition and subtraction in H gene regulatory networks
sec.p: In this section, we are going to show how two patterned gene products in a hierarchic network can lead to more complex patterns in downstream gene products without requiring additional extracellular signals. This can be achieved by two simple mechanisms that include positive (for ‘addition’ of patterns) and negative (for ‘subtraction’ of patterns) intracellular regulations between the patterned gene products.

Let us consider two gene products i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} exhibiting heterogeneous resulting patterns g¯i(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{i}\left (x\right)$\end{document} and g¯j(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{j}\left (x\right)$\end{document} that directly regulate intracellular gene product k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}. If no other gene product in the network regulates k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}, its concentration dynamics for each x\begin{document}$x$\end{document} is given by:(S5.1)∂tgk(t,x)=fk(gi(x),gj(t,x))+μkgk(t,x);\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \partial _{t}g_{k}\left (t,x\right)=f_{k}\left (g_{i}\left (x\right),g_{j}\left (t,x\right)\right)+\mu _{k}g_{k}\left (t,x\right);$$\end{document}

and then, assuming that i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} reach their respective stationary concentrations fast enough, we can take the time derivative in Equation S5.1 equal to zero and get that the stationary concentration of gene product k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} is given by:(S5.2)g¯k(x)=1μkfk(g¯i(x),g¯j(x)).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \bar{g}_{k}\left (x\right)=\frac{1}{\mu _{k}}f_{k}\left (\bar{g}_{i}\left (x\right),\bar{g}_{j}\left (x\right)\right).$$\end{document}

First, we consider the case of the peak addition mechanism, i.e., we assume that both i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} positively regulate gene product k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} (see Figure 11 in the main text). In this case, according to requirement R5 in the main text, fk(gi,gj)\begin{document}$f_{k}\left (g_{i},g_{j}\right)$\end{document} is component-wise monotonically increasing with respect to both gi\begin{document}$g_{i}$\end{document} and gj\begin{document}$g_{j}$\end{document}. Hence, we know that the stationary concentration of gene product k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} will increase wherever the stationary concentrations of both i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} simultaneously increase; and it will decrease wherever those of i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} simultaneously decrease. As a result, if both g¯i(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{i}\left (x\right)$\end{document} and g¯j(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{j}\left (x\right)$\end{document} have a concentration peak at the same position x^\begin{document}$\hat {x}$\end{document}, then g¯k(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{k}\left (x\right)$\end{document} will also exhibit a peak at x^\begin{document}$\hat {x}$\end{document}.

Ambiguity appears in those cases for which the peaks of concentration of i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} do not coincide at the same spatial position. In this sense, let us assume that the stationary concentrations of gene products i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} exhibit a total amount of N\begin{document}$N$\end{document} and M\begin{document}$M$\end{document} concentration peaks along the domain, respectively; and let us focus on two consecutive such peaks, i.e., let us consider a concentration peak in g¯i(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{i}\left (x\right)$\end{document} located at a given position x^i\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{i}$\end{document} and a concentration peak in g¯j(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{j}\left (x\right)$\end{document} at a different position x^j≠x^i\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{j} \neq \hat {x}_{i}$\end{document} such that neither gi¯(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g_{i}}\left (x\right)$\end{document} nor gj¯(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g_{j}}\left (x\right)$\end{document} exhibit an intermediate concentration peak between x^i\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{i}$\end{document} and x^j\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{j}$\end{document}. In this setting, if x^i\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{i}$\end{document} and x^j\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{j}$\end{document} are far enough from each other and both concentration peaks are steep enough so that the influence of g¯j(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{j}\left (x\right)$\end{document} (resp., g¯i(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{i}\left (x\right)$\end{document}) is negligible near x^i\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{i}$\end{document} (resp., x^j\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{j}$\end{document}); then, fk(gi,gj)\begin{document}$f_{k}\left (g_{i},g_{j}\right)$\end{document} will behave as a function of only gi\begin{document}$g_{i}$\end{document} (resp., gj\begin{document}$g_{j}$\end{document}) in a vicinity of x^i\begin{document}$\overset{\hat }{x}_{i}$\end{document} (resp., x^j\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{j}$\end{document}) and thus, g¯k(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{k}\left (x\right)$\end{document} will exhibit one concentration peak at x^i\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{i}$\end{document} and another concentration peak at x^j\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{j}$\end{document}. Moreover, if this condition holds for any pair of consecutive peaks of g¯i(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{i}\left (x\right)$\end{document} and g¯j(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{j}\left (x\right)$\end{document}, g¯k(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{k}\left (x\right)$\end{document} will exhibit a total amount of N+M\begin{document}$N+M$\end{document} concentration peaks along the domain (see Figure 11 in the main text). On the contrary, if two such consecutive peaks of i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} are too close to each other, the expected concentration peaks of k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} may merge into just one located between x^i\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{i}$\end{document} and x^j\begin{document}$\hat {x}_{j}$\end{document}, and then, the total number of concentration peaks that k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} will exhibit along the domain is strictly smaller than N+M\begin{document}$N+M$\end{document}.

On the other hand, let us consider the case of the peak subtraction mechanism, i.e., let us assume that i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} activates k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} while j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} inhibits it (see Figure 11 in the main text). In this setting, according to requirement R5 in the main text, fk(gi,gj)\begin{document}$f_{k}\left (g_{i},g_{j}\right)$\end{document} is monotonically increasing with respect to gi\begin{document}$g_{i}$\end{document} and monotonically decreasing with respect to gj\begin{document}$g_{j}$\end{document}. As in the case of peak addition, let us assume that the stationary concentrations of gene products i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} display a total amount of N\begin{document}$N$\end{document} concentration peaks each. Also, let us assume that two such peaks of concentration coincide at the same position x^\begin{document}$\hat{x}$\end{document}. Then, if the activation of i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} on k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} is much stronger than the inhibition of j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} on k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}, g¯k(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{k}\left (x\right)$\end{document} will portray a concentration peak at x^\begin{document}$\hat {x}$\end{document}. Conversely, if the inhibition of j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} on k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} is much stronger than the activation of i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} on k\begin{document}$k$\end{document}, no concentration peak of k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} will emerge at x^\begin{document}$\hat {x}$\end{document}. Thus, if the former situation takes place at all possible pairs of concentration peaks of i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document}, g¯k(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{k}\left (x\right)$\end{document} will display a total amount of N\begin{document}$N$\end{document} concentration peaks along the domain. However, if the latter situation takes place for all possible pairs of peaks, gk¯(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g_{k}}\left (x\right)$\end{document} will retract back to a homogeneous concentration as all possible peaks of concentration will be eventually swept away by the inhibition of j\begin{document}$j$\end{document}.

However, as we have seen in S3: Gradients of extracellular signals from spikes, under some specific conditions on function f and specific parameter values, the inhibition that j\begin{document}$j$\end{document} exerts on k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} can split the emerging concentration peak in two in such a way that, on a 1D domain, g¯k(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{k}\left (x\right)$\end{document} displays two symmetric concentration peaks on both sides of x^\begin{document}$\hat {x}$\end{document} (this pair of symmetric peaks becomes a ring around x^\begin{document}$\hat{x}$\end{document} in 2D and a hollow sphere in 3D). Moreover, this split would also be the case even if the concentration peaks in g¯i(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{i}\left (x\right)$\end{document} and g¯j(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{j}\left (x\right)$\end{document} did not coincide at the same position, but stand in close positions (although in this case the height of the emerging peaks in gk¯(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g_{k}}\left (x\right)$\end{document} would be uneven). Anyhow, if this splitting of peaks occurs for all possible pairs of concentration peaks of i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and j\begin{document}$j$\end{document}, g¯k(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{k}\left (x\right)$\end{document} will exhibit a total amount of 2N\begin{document}$2N$\end{document} peaks along the 1D domain (in higher dimensions, each pair of peaks reduces to one single ring or sphere and hence, the total amount of structures in g¯k(x)\begin{document}$\bar{g}_{k}\left (x\right)$\end{document} reduces to N\begin{document}$N$\end{document}).

sec.title: S6: Numerical simulations
sec.p: In this subsection, we provide the necessary information to reproduce the numerical simulations leading to all resulting patterns presented in the various figures along the main text. Hence, we first offer a detailed description of the Maini-Miura model (Miura and Maini, 2004; Marcon et al., 2016), which serves as the basis for the reaction-diffusion equations in all our simulations (i.e. Equation 1 of the main text), and we list the specific parameter values applied in each case. All parameters presented in this supplementary section are expressed in arbitrary units (a.u.).

sec.title: The Maini-Miura model
sec.p: In all our simulations, the underlying reaction-diffusion equations correspond to the Maini-Miura model (Miura and Maini, 2004; Marcon et al., 2016) or slight modifications of it. The governing equations of this simple model of pattern formation are given by:(S6.1)∂tg(t,x)=W⊤(g(t,x)−g*)−S(g(t,x)−g*)3−M(g(t,x)−g*)+D∇2g(t,x),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \partial _{t}\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right)=\boldsymbol{W}^{\top}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right)-\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\right)-\boldsymbol{S}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right)-\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\right)^{\boldsymbol{3}}-\boldsymbol{M}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right)-\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\right)+\boldsymbol{D}{\nabla }^{2}\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right),$$\end{document}

where g(t,x)∈RNg\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right)\in \mathbb{R}^{N_{g}}$\end{document} is the vector of gene product concentrations at time t≥0\begin{document}$t\geq 0$\end{document} and position x\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{x}$\end{document}; g*∈RNg\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\in \mathbb{R}^{N_{g}}$\end{document} is a homogeneous steady-state concentration; W∈RNg×Ng\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{W}\in \mathbb{R}^{N_{g}\times N_{g}}$\end{document} is the weight matrix of the corresponding gene regulatory network; S=diag(σ1,...,σNg)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{S}=\text{diag}\left (\sigma _{1},...,\sigma _{N_{g}}\right)$\end{document} is the cubic saturation matrix; M=diag(μ1,...,μNg)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{M}=\text{diag}\left (\mu _{1},...,\mu _{N_{g}}\right)$\end{document} is the linear degradation matrix; and D=diag(d1,...,dNg)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{D}=\text{diag}\left (d_{1},...,d_{N_{g}}\right)$\end{document} is the diffusion matrix. As in Equation 1 of the main text, g3\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}^{\boldsymbol{3}}$\end{document} denotes component-wise exponentiation.

Function f(g)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{f}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\right)$\end{document} in Equation 1 of the main text corresponds to the combination of terms W⊤(g(t,x)−g*)−S(g(t,x)−g*)3+Mg*\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{W}^{\top}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right)-\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\right)-\boldsymbol{S}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right)-\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\right)^{\boldsymbol{3}}+\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}$\end{document} in Equation S6.1. Given its polynomial structure, it is straightforward to check that it satisfies requirements R1 and R3 in the main text and, if σi>0\begin{document}$\sigma _{i} \gt 0$\end{document} for at least one gene product, also requirement R2. The Jacobian matrix of f(g)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{f}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\right)$\end{document} at g*\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}$\end{document} coincides with the transpose weight matrix (i.e. Jf(g*)=W⊤\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{J}_{\boldsymbol{f}}\left (\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\right)=\boldsymbol{W}^{\top}$\end{document}) and then, f(g)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{f}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\right)$\end{document} satisfies requirement R5 in the main text by continuity (at least in a neighborhood of g*\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}$\end{document}). Regarding requirement R4 in the main text, concentration g(t,x)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right)$\end{document} in the Maini-Miura model is always bounded from above because for large values of g(t,x)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right)$\end{document} both degradation terms in Equation S6.1 become negative. Also, the entries in g*\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}$\end{document} can be tuned to avoid g(t,x)<0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right) \lt 0$\end{document} for all time t≥0\begin{document}$t\geq 0$\end{document} and all positions x\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{x}$\end{document}.

Despite its many simplifications, the Maini-Miura model offers a practical framework for the study of pattern formation governed by gene regulatory networks, as its formulation enables a direct manipulation of gene network topology by simply changing the entries of the weight matrix W\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{W}$\end{document}. This adaptability makes the Maini-Miura model particularly suitable for the study of gene regulatory networks comprising a large number of gene products, unlike classical models such as the Schnackenberg (Schnakenberg, 1979; Murray, 2002) or Gierer-Meinhardt models (Gierer and Meinhardt, 1972; Meinhardt, 1982), which are constrained to a very specific 2-node Turing gene network.

In our simulations, we build spike, spike-homogeneous, and noise-homogeneous initial patterns using g*\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}$\end{document} as their basal concentrations. For spike- and noise-homogeneous initial patterns, we consider gi*>0\begin{document}$g_{i}^{\text{*}} \gt 0$\end{document} big enough so that gi(t,x)\begin{document}$g_{i}\left (t,x\right)$\end{document} never becomes negative. For spike initial patterns, we take g*≡0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\equiv 0$\end{document} and clamp possible negative concentrations by introducing a smooth step function in the first term of Equation S6.1:(S6.2)f(g)=Φ(ε)(W⊤(g(t,x)−g*)−S(g(t,x)−g*)3+Mg*),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol{f}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\right)=\boldsymbol{\Phi} ^{\left (\varepsilon \right)}\left (\boldsymbol{W}^{\top}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\left (t,\boldsymbol{x}\right)-\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\right)-\boldsymbol{S}\left(\boldsymbol{g}(t,\boldsymbol{x})-\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\right)^{\boldsymbol{3}}+\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\right),$$\end{document}

where each entry Φij(ε)(z)=(1+e−z/ε)−1\begin{document}$\Phi _{ij}^{\left (\varepsilon \right)}\left (z\right)=\left (1+e^{-z/\varepsilon }\right)^{-1}$\end{document} is a narrow sigmoid function, with ε>0\begin{document}$\varepsilon \gt 0$\end{document} arbitrarily small. Note that the inclusion of the smooth step function Φ(ε)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{\Phi} ^{\left (\varepsilon \right)}$\end{document} in f(g)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{f}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\right)$\end{document} is consistent with requirements R1–R5 in the main text. Moreover, if we choose ε\begin{document}$\varepsilon $\end{document} small enough, it acts as an effective clamping term in model equations that prevents the occurrence of negative concentrations during the simulations.

In a similar spirit, several figures in the main text and the supplementary information explicitly require different components of f(g)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{f}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\right)$\end{document} to adopt different functional forms (e.g. Figure 8 in the main text, evaluating conditions RH1 and RH2). In such simulations, only some specific components of f(g)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{f}\left (\boldsymbol{g}\right)$\end{document} are modified, leaving all remaining terms of Equation S6.1 unchanged. Each such modification is listed below, together with the corresponding set of model parameters that lead to the pattern transformation under consideration.

sec.title: Parameter values for patterning simulations
sec.p: All simulations in this article have been performed using a Forward-Euler algorithm (Grossmann and Ross, 2007) on a 1D interval [0,50]\begin{document}$\left [0,50\right ]$\end{document} split into a line array of 500 cells with a constant spatial step (i.e. distance between cell centers) of h=0.1\begin{document}$h=0.1$\end{document} or a 2D square [0,50]×[0,50]\begin{document}$\left [0,50\right ]\times \left [0,50\right ]$\end{document} split into a square ensemble of 250 × 250 cells with a constant spatial step of h=0.1\begin{document}$h=0.1$\end{document}. The time step τ\begin{document}$\tau $\end{document} of the algorithm is adjusted for every simulation in such a way that the convergence condition of the Forward-Euler algorithm is satisfied for all gene products in the gene network (i.e. 2nτdi<h2\begin{document}$2^{n}\tau d_{i} \lt h^{2}$\end{document} for all i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and n=1,2\begin{document}$n=1,2$\end{document}). This results in a D\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{D}$\end{document}-dependent time step of the form:(S6.3)τ=τ(D)=h2(2n+0.1)max{d1,...,dNg}, for n=1,2.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tau =\tau \left (\boldsymbol{D}\right)=\frac{h^{2}}{\left (2^{n}+0.1\right)max\left \{d_{1},...,d_{N_{g}}\right \}},\text{ for }n=1,2.$$\end{document}

All simulations start with an initial pattern built around the equilibrium point of Equation S6.1, i.e., g*=(g1*,...,gNg*)⊤\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}=\left (g_{1}^{\text{*}},...,g_{N_{g}}^{\text{*}}\right)^{\top}$\end{document}. Spike (g*=0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}=0$\end{document}) and spike-homogeneous (g*≠0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{g}^{\text{*}}\neq 0$\end{document}) initial conditions centered at x0∈Rn\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\in \mathbb{R}^{n}$\end{document} are given by rectangular functions of the form:(S6.4)gi(0,x)=gi*+Airect(||x−x0||2L),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle g_{i}\left (0,\boldsymbol{x}\right)=g_{i}^{\text{*}}+A_{i}\,\text{rect}\left (\frac{||\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_{0}||_{2}}{L}\right),$$\end{document}

where Ai>0\begin{document}$A_{i} \gt 0$\end{document} is the amplitude of the spike; L>0\begin{document}$L \gt 0$\end{document} is the width of the spike (equal for all gene products); ||⋅||2\begin{document}$||\cdot ||_{2}$\end{document} denotes the Euclidean norm; and rect(y)=1\begin{document}$\text{rect}\left (y\right)=1$\end{document}, if -1≤y≤1\begin{document}$-1\leq y\leq 1$\end{document}, while rect(y)=0\begin{document}$\text{rect}\left (y\right)=0$\end{document}, elsewhere (Abramowitz and Stegun, 1964).
